questions: For permitted but time- or chance-dependent implementations, is AdmissionVerdict defined as the permanently cached result of the first sampled admission, or must admission establish deterministic behavior (and refuse or otherwise handle an implementation whose verdict could differ on another execution)?
What does “deterministic verdict” mean when an admitted implementation may produce different results on repeated executions of the same corpus?

judgement.why: P1 judged the same question about admission of time- or chance-dependent implementations under the unchanged recorded-verdict reuse rule.

precedent.topic: How admission verdicts are deterministic when implementations can access time or randomness
quotes:
2. Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs
   admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the
   current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used. The
   corpus digest is the content identity (State 6, decision 14) of the list of
   its `trial_case_id`s in corpus order.
   Admission executes the implementation on every case of the corpus, in corpus
   order, each as one TrialExecution M07, and never stops early — save for an
   execution whose cleanup cannot be confirmed: it is recorded `crashed` with
   `cleanup_failed` and the kernel stops (A03 rule 7), with no verdict
   recorded; after the restart a submission runs admission afresh.

3. A case passes when the execution succeeded and, if the case states expected
   outputs, every output's digest equals the expected one — a file output is
   recorded in the TrialExecution by digest, size and media type, keeps no bytes,
   and is compared with the expected file fixture by digest; a `many` file output
   equals its expected list when both have the same length and the digests are
   equal position by position, so order and repetitions count; outputs that
   validate but differ are `output_mismatch`. The verdict is `admitted` exactly
   when the corpus is non-empty and every case passed; otherwise `refused` with
   reason `empty_corpus`, or with the first case in corpus order that did not
   pass and its outcome.
precedent.why: State 2 decides that the first admission executes the corpus and records the verdict determined by those observed executions, while later submissions of the same implementation and corpus digest reuse that recorded verdict.

topics.topic: Whether function implementations must be pure and nondeterminism is forbidden
questions: Is an implementation that obtains time or randomness through a route the sandbox does not detect a valid function eligible for admission, or is it forbidden because function implementations must be pure?

judgement.why: P2 judged the same question about whether undetected time- or chance-dependent code remains eligible for admission under the unchanged purity passages.

precedent.topic: Whether implementation purity is required or merely approximated by blocking known time and randomness APIs
quotes:
The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.
precedent.why: The changed passage expressly says alternate time or chance access is not detected and the code is judged by its observed outputs, so passing such code is not refused merely for that undetected dependency.

topics.topic: Which TrialCase facts contribute to corpus_digest
questions: From what model facts is corpus_digest minted: only the active TrialCase identities/content, or also TrialCase provenance and record facts such as origin, captured_from, added_by and added_at?
